newsitem.title: MONACO: RALLYING-MAKINEN LEADS AS MCRAE CRASHES OUT.
newsitem.headline: RALLYING-MAKINEN LEADS AS MCRAE CRASHES OUT.

text.p: World champion Tommi Makinen of Finland captured the lead in the Monte Carlo Rally on Tuesday but still faces tough competition from Piero Liatti and Carlos Sainz in the opening event of the season.
It was a bad day, however, for Briton Colin McRae, who crashed out of the race after starting the day in fourth position.

Mitsubishi driver Makinen, who began the penultimate day three seconds behind the Spaniard Sainz, drove brilliantly to end the day with a 24-second lead over Italy's Liatti. Sainz was third, a further three seconds back.

Liatti shone on wet roads with icy patches in the Vercors mountains, taking three of the day's six tests in his Subaru Impreza. But Makinen won two and was never more than a handful of seconds behind in the others.

With Liatti's Subaru and Sainz, driving a Ford Escort, both pressing hard, the gifted Finn took every conceivable risk to clinch the day's last timed stage over 18.6 kms from Plan de Vitrolles to Sigoyer.
He gained 14 seconds on Liatti and 18 on Sainz in that stage alone, as if underlining his determination to keep the number one spot when the rally ends on Wednesday in Monte Carlo.
It also gave him a psychological edge over his two rivals.
"I'm doing my best and I'm not far back but Makinen is so consistent that it will be very difficult," admitted Liatti.
Sainz was equally pessimistic: "I've had a few problems with my brakes but apart from that, everything went smoothly," he said.
"I thing I'm doing fine but it looks like other guys are doing even better."

Meanwhile McRae, who had dropped to fourth place overall after hitting a snowdrift on Monday, had to pull out after going off the road again in his Subaru in Tuesday's first timed stage, a 33-km run from St Jean en Royans to La Chapelle en Vercors.
"We hit a patch of ice on my side and went off into the snowbank," McRae explained.
"We lost of a lot of time to get the car out. We managed to finish the stage but the front left steering arm broke and it was impossible to continue."
The day also ruined the hopes of three-times winner Didier Auriol, who was dreaming of matching the record of four wins in the winter classic set by Italian Sandro Munari and German Walter Roehrl.
Frenchman Auriol was fifth overall in his privately-entered Ford Escort with two tests remaining in the day when gearbox problems forced him to retire.

Makinen also sensed trouble when a warning light came up on his dashboard during the day's fourth test over 27.47 kms from Ruissas to Eygalayes. But that still did not stop him from setting the best time.
"It kept flashing for the whole stage," he said. "Don't ask me what it was, I just don't know."
Six more timed stages await the drivers as they leave the mountains to return to the principality on Wednesday.

New formats for shorter rallies mean that the organisers have scrapped the traditional night finale and the race will end just after dark, as it began on Sunday, with a test using the lower part of the Monaco Grand Prix circuit.
